units.text: Don't give exclusivity away before it is earned: sign a nonexclusive OEM pilot now and make North American exclusivity conditional on certification and audited volumes
Decision question (Board of Directors, April 2027 decision): should Boreal grant North American exclusivity to an OEM for its industrial robot navigation software in 2027?
Board pre-read prepared November 2026 from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data). All $ figures are undiscounted; no NPV is computed, as the board requested.

Decline Option X as drafted. Sign Option N, a 12-month nonexclusive pilot at $350 per robot, and agree up front the gates under which Option M (limited exclusivity) takes effect: certification passed, two audited quarters at about 9,000 robots a year, and contract protections signed.

The deal is worth less than it is being presented as: the $2.0M is a recoupable advance on royalties, not extra revenue; three-year OEM cash is $8.7M, not the $10.7M the 'revenue win' framing implies.

After $80/robot support, $0.9M/yr engineering, the $0.45M assessment and displaced direct sales, exclusivity over 2027–29 is worth +$2.2M to +$2.8M at plan volumes but only −$0.04M to +$0.55M if the OEM ships 65% of plan.

units.text: The evidence the board requires for irreversible exclusivity does not exist yet: lab uptime is 98.8% against a 99.5% production bar.
The third-party assessment has not started. OEM volumes are unaudited, and the 14,000 'booked devices' are a forecast.
The growth claim rests on correlation.
The draft lacks audit rights, a royalty floor, release triggers and code escrow.

The phased N→M structure beats every alternative: it earns $50 more per robot, keeps the direct channel (~$1.48M of gross margin on new ARR in 2028), and matches X's value even if the OEM ships 24–32% fewer robots.
N→M holds cash at least $0.55M above the $2.6M buffer in the worst case, and it fails none of the board's conditions.
Start the $0.45M assessment now; it is on the critical path for every OEM route.
Convert to exclusivity only after certification and audited shipments of at least 2,250 robots a quarter.
If the OEM insists on exclusivity at signing, walk away and fall back to direct sales plus the integration-firm pilot.
Of six conditions that would have to hold for exclusivity at signing to be right, only one partly holds, so the 'don't sign yet' hypothesis stands.

Initial hypothesis (stated before testing): Boreal should not grant exclusivity at signing; a nonexclusive or milestone deal captures the OEM upside without giving up the direct channel. Test: state what must hold for the opposite answer (Option X) to be right, then check each condition against the pack.

Condition 1 (Value): 'The $2.0M signing payment adds value on top of royalties' — Does not hold. It is an advance credited against the first $2.0M of royalties, and the partner can demand an offset. 3-yr cash is $8.7M either way.

Condition 2 (Value): 'Exclusivity creates value even in the low case and with realistic channel overlap' — Partly: plan case only. +$2.2–2.8M at plan; −$0.04M to +$0.55M at 65% volumes with Sales' 30–70% overlap.

Condition 3 (Evidence): 'The product is production-ready in the OEM's hardware' — Does not hold. 98.8% lab uptime vs 99.5% required; no loaded-warehouse or collision-heavy test; assessment not started.

Condition 4 (Evidence): 'OEM volumes and the growth story are reliable enough to commit on' — Does not hold. Shipments unaudited; '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders; competitor evidence is correlational.
Condition 5 (Alternatives): 'Exclusivity is the only way to win the OEM's volume' — Does not hold. The OEM will consider Option N (nonexclusive, $350/robot) and Option M (gated exclusivity).
Condition 6 (Protection): 'The contract protects Boreal if forecasts or certification miss' — Does not hold. No audit right, no royalty floor after the advance, no release triggers, no code escrow.
Result: the hypothesis survives, refined. The problem is exclusivity before evidence, not exclusivity itself, so the answer is a gated path to exclusivity rather than a flat 'no'.
Plan 2027: 5,000 robots shipped; royalties earned ($300) 1.50; advance credit applied −1.50; royalty cash received 0.00; total OEM cash incl. $2.0M at signing 2.00 ($M).
Plan 2028: 10,000 robots; royalties earned 3.00; advance credit applied −0.50; royalty cash received 2.50; total OEM cash 2.50 ($M).
Plan 2029: 14,000 robots; royalties earned 4.20; advance credit 0.00; royalty cash received 4.20; total OEM cash 4.20 ($M).
Plan total: 29,000 robots; royalties earned 8.70; advance credit −2.00; royalty cash received 6.70; total OEM cash incl. $2.0M at signing 8.70 ($M).
65% stress 2027: 3,250 robots; royalties earned 0.98; advance credit −0.98; royalty cash 0.00; total OEM cash 2.00 ($M).
65% stress 2028: 6,500 robots; royalties earned 1.95; advance credit −1.03; royalty cash 0.93; total OEM cash 0.93 ($M).
65% stress 2029: 9,100 robots; royalties earned 2.73; advance credit 0.00; royalty cash 2.73; total OEM cash 2.73 ($M).
Stress total: 18,850 robots; royalties earned 5.66; advance credit −2.00; royalty cash 3.66; total OEM cash 5.66 ($M).
How the board should describe it: Revenue = royalties earned as qualifying robots ship and payment is collected: $1.5M in 2027 at plan, not $3.5M.
The $2.0M is a minimum-guarantee liability until it is earned. The partner can demand an offset if guaranteed performance is missed.
The 'revenue win plus recurring royalties' framing double-counts $2.0M, overstating 3-year OEM income by 23% ($10.7M vs $8.7M).
What the advance buys: timing only. It brings $1.5–2.0M of cash forward into 2027, which Boreal does not need to stay above its buffer.

Reading the table: the advance is cash received early, then netted out of 2028 royalty cash. Total cash therefore always equals royalties earned. In the stress case, 2028 royalty cash falls to $0.93M because $1.03M of credit is still being recouped.
After full costs, $3.00M of 2028 plan royalties shrinks to about $0.56M of incremental value, 19% rather than the dashboard's 100%.

2028 plan waterfall ($M): royalties 3.0 (10,000 × $300); variable support 0.8 (10,000 × $80); OEM-specific engineering 0.9; OEM contribution 1.3; displaced direct gross margin 0.738; incremental value 0.562.
CFO dashboard: 100% margin. It counts only the $300 royalty.
Per robot: $220 (73%) after $80 of support, before any fixed cost.
Complete incremental view: ~19% at plan. That is $0.27–0.86M across 30–70% overlap.
At 65% volumes it turns negative: $1.95M − $0.52M − $0.90M − $0.74M = −$0.21M in 2028.
Exclusivity bars all new direct North American licences, including customers who buy other OEMs' robots. That forgone margin is a real cost of Option X, not of the OEM channel in general.
Lost direct margin = 50% (midpoint of Sales' 30–70% overlap) × $1.8M ARR × 82% gross margin.
Option X three-year incremental value, $M = Σ(royalties − $80 × robots − $0.9M engineering) − $0.45M assessment − overlap × ($1.8M × 82%).
Panel A: direct cohort counted in 2028 only (pack-grounded floor; favours Option X).
Panel A, Plan (29,000 robots): 0% overlap (CEO view) +3.23; 30% (Sales low) +2.79; 50% (midpoint) +2.49; 70% (Sales high) +2.20; 100% (all displaced) +1.75 ($M).
Even on the most favourable reading, the low case leaves at most $0.55M of value for three years of irreversible exclusivity.
Panel B sensitivity (lost 2028 direct customers would also have renewed in 2029; churn not in pack), Plan (29,000): 0% +3.23; 30% +2.34; 50% +1.75; 70% +1.16; 100% +0.28 ($M).
If direct ARR renews, as recurring revenue normally does, the low case destroys up to $1.1M at Sales' 70% overlap.
Costs assume full-year engineering from 2027, which is conservative. If deployments start late in 2027, all OEM options gain equally and the ranking does not change.
Exclusivity breaks even only if the OEM ships 6,100–8,800 robots a year; the 65% case (6,500 in 2028) barely clears the most optimistic end.
Breakeven robots per year by overlap: 0% 4,091; 30% 6,104; 50% 7,445; 70% 8,787; 100% 10,800; against OEM 2028 at 65% stress 6,500 and partner plan 10,000.
Grey bars show the annual OEM shipments needed for exclusivity to beat staying nonexclusive.
units.correct_version: Grey bars show the annual OEM shipments needed for exclusivity (Option X terms) to beat having no OEM deal, i.e. direct sales only. The breakeven formula (($0.9M + overlap × $1.476M) ÷ $220) does not compare against the nonexclusive option; on the deck's own numbers N beats X at any equal volume, so the ~9,000/yr gate shows exclusivity is value-positive against direct-only, not that it beats continuing N.

units.text: Each robot contributes $220, which must cover $0.9M of engineering plus the displaced direct margin. Breakeven = ($0.9M + overlap × $1.476M) ÷ ($300 − $80).
At Sales' 30–70% overlap, the hurdle is 6,100–8,800 robots a year. The plan (10,000) clears it; the stress case (6,500) clears only the 30% end.
Option M's proposed gate of 5,000 annualised is below every realistic breakeven. It should rise to about 9,000 (2,250 per quarter) unless the scope excludes customers on other OEMs' robots.
Under Option N, the OEM programme alone breaks even at 3,333 robots ($0.9M ÷ $270), and the direct channel is untouched.
The software has not yet met the OEM's production bar, and Option X would make exclusivity binding at signing, about five months before certification at the earliest.
Lab uptime 98.8% (60 robots, 12 weeks) vs OEM production acceptance bar 99.5%.
Downtime cut still needed: −58% (105 → 44 h per robot-year); Downtime cut = 1 − (0.5% ÷ 1.2%) = 58%; downtime hours assume 24/7 operation (8,760 h/yr).
Not yet demonstrated: safe-stop performance in a fully loaded warehouse; collision-heavy peak conditions (not in the trial); uptime in the OEM's production hardware, not the lab.
Third-party security and safety assessment ($0.45M): not started.
Certification by September 2027 is an engineering projection, not a plan with a vendor in place.

Option X timing against the board's own condition: Nov 2026 today, assessment not started; Apr 2027 board meets, under X exclusivity binds here; Sep 2027 earliest certification (projected); Dec 2027 plan assumes 5,000 robots shipped in 2027.
The board requires documented uptime and safety validation in OEM hardware before irreversible exclusivity. Option X fails that condition by design.
Production deployment cannot start until the assessment is complete, so the 2027 plan of 5,000 robots is at risk, and with it the advance's offset exposure.

The gap is closable but unproven: to reach 99.5%, downtime must fall from 1.2% to 0.5% of hours. Over the 12-week trial that means about 24 → 10 hours per robot, under harsher conditions than the lab.
The upside case rests on unaudited volumes, an untested 'fully incremental' claim and a correlational competitor analogy.
OEM volumes are a forecast, not a commitment: quarterly shipment data are not independently audited, and the draft contract has no audit right.
The '14,000 booked devices' have no purchase orders. Treat them as a 2029 forecast.
The 2027 forecast of 5,000 assumes production shipments in a year when certification lands in September at the earliest.
The board is unwilling to rely solely on verbal OEM launch forecasts.

Channel overlap is unknown, and it drives the answer: the CEO says the OEM channel is 0% overlap (entirely incremental). Sales says 30–70% of OEM buyers overlap with its pipeline. Neither view is backed by customer-level identifiers.
Each 10 points of overlap is worth ~$0.15M a year of displaced direct gross margin ($1.8M × 82% × 10%).
The overlap can be measured during a nonexclusive pilot. It cannot be measured after exclusivity has closed the direct channel.

'Exclusivity caused competitors' growth' is not shown: five competitors' exclusive OEM deals coincided with faster growth. That is a correlation. Those firms had more marketing support, more mature products and higher market share before they signed, so any of these could explain the growth.
Boreal has none of these advantages yet: its product is uncertified and its leverage limited.
No causal evidence is available, so we give this argument zero weight in the economics.
Impact: plan → 65% moves 3-yr value by −$2.2M.
Impact: 30% → 70% overlap moves the breakeven from 6,100 to 8,800 robots/yr.
Impact: no evidence that exclusivity itself adds volume over N.
As drafted, the contract leaves Boreal exposed on six terms, and its scope blocks the growing direct channel.

Audit rights — draft: no clear right to audit reported shipments; risk: royalties and volume gates rest on unaudited OEM reports; required before any exclusivity: independent, shipment-level audit right; quarterly reports reconciled to invoices.
Royalty floor — draft: none once the $2.0M advance is used up; risk: direct channel barred with no minimum income; required: annual minimum royalty; exclusivity lapses automatically if missed.
Release triggers — draft: no automatic release; risk: locked in if the model is retired or certification slips; required: automatic release on model retirement, certification slip or missed minimums.

IP protection — draft: source code delivered as freely reusable OEM IP; risk: loss of Boreal's core asset and future leverage; required: source code escrow with narrow release conditions; no IP transfer.

Scope — draft: all new North American sales, including customers on other OEMs' robots; risk: chief strategic opportunity cost; ~$1.48M/yr of direct margin at risk; required: limit to the OEM's robot series; carve out existing and other-OEM customers.

Guarantee offset — draft: partner can demand an offset if guaranteed performance is missed; risk: the $2.0M can claw back, e.g. if certification delays 2027 shipments; required: define the offset; cap it at the unearned balance; no offset for OEM-driven shortfalls.
Existing direct contracts cannot be terminated for convenience. Any exclusivity must apply only to future new North American robot sales, or Boreal faces unquantified contract claims.
Of the five routes, the phased N→M structure is the only one that keeps the OEM upside without an irreversible bet before the evidence exists.

X: exclusive at signing — indicative value 2027–29 +$2.2–2.8M plan; −$0.04 to +$0.55M at 65%; low-case resilience weak (thin margin, offset exposure); reversibility none (3 years, binding at signing); fails the validation-first board condition; deal risk lowest (it is the OEM's ask). Verdict: Reject as drafted.

N: 12-month nonexclusive pilot — up to +$4.7M plan / +$1.9M at 65% if terms hold (upper bound); low-case resilience strong (no guarantee to recoup; $270/robot); reversibility high (12 months); meets all board conditions; deal risk medium (offered by the OEM; price not guaranteed). Verdict: Recommend: phase 1.

M: exclusivity after gates — X-like upside, taken only once proven; low-case resilience strong (gates screen out the low case); reversibility high until the gates are met; meets all board conditions; deal risk medium (termination payment still open). Verdict: Recommend: phase 2.
Direct sales only — keeps ~$1.48M/yr direct margin on 2028 new ARR; no OEM upside; low-case resilience strong; reversibility high; meets all board conditions; forgoes the OEM. Verdict: Fallback.

Defer until certified — as direct, less the $0.45M assessment; low-case resilience strong; reversibility high; meets all board conditions; deal risk high (OEM may choose another supplier). Verdict: Fallback if N refused.
Board conditions: validation in OEM hardware before irreversible exclusivity; existing licences protected; $2.6M liquidity buffer held.

The integration firm's 1,200-robot nonexclusive pilot is a complement to N and to the fallbacks; X would likely bar it, as it covers new customers on other OEMs' robots. Its royalty terms are not in the pack (treated as a nonexclusive complement, not valued).
Nonexclusive terms would match exclusivity's value even if the OEM shipped 24–32% fewer robots without exclusivity.
Three-year value ($M), partner plan (29,000 robots) / 65% stress (18,850 robots): X at 30% overlap 2.79 / 0.55; X at 70% overlap 2.2 / −0.04; N terms, same volumes 4.68 / 1.94.
Why N wins on value per unit of risk: N pays $350 vs $300 per robot ($270 vs $220 after support) and does not displace the direct channel.
N matches X's three-year value at 22,000 robots (30% overlap) or 19,800 (70%), against the 29,000 plan: 24–32% fewer robots. N parity volume = (X value + $2.7M + $0.45M) ÷ ($350 − $80).
In the stress case the cushion is 27–39%.

Caveats: the OEM may ship less without exclusivity, and it will not guarantee final pricing. Some OEM buyers would also substitute for direct buyers under N. The N bars are an upper bound; the volume cushion is the robust finding.
N assumes its $350 terms and partner volumes persist for 3 years, which the OEM has not guaranteed (favours N; shown as an upper bound).
Every route keeps cash above the $2.6M buffer; the advance's liquidity benefit is temporary and can be clawed back.

Headroom above $2.6M buffer, end-2027 ($M): Direct sales only 2.3; Defer: assessment only 1.85; N: royalties collected in-year 2.3; N: worst case, no 2027 royalty cash (lag) 0.55; X: plan, advance in hand 2.55; X: certification slips, $2.0M offset 1.85.
Start: $4.9M cash − $2.6M buffer = $2.3M headroom.
OEM routes spend the $0.45M assessment, $0.9M of engineering and $80/robot of support ($0.40M at 5,000 robots) before royalty cash arrives.
N's tightest point is $0.55M, if reporting lags push all 2027 royalties into 2028. Mitigations: monthly remittance, engineering phased to shipments, OEM-funded integration work.
X looks richest ($2.55M), but only because the advance is unearned. A certification slip plus an offset demand takes it back to $1.85M.
Liquidity does not require the advance. It is not a reason to sign X.
Headroom = $4.9M cash − $2.6M buffer + deal cash flows to end-2027. Rest-of-business burn is not in the pack and is assumed to be covered by the buffer.
Recommendation: sign Option N now and pre-agree three gates that switch on limited exclusivity (Option M) once certification and audited volumes show it pays.

Phase 0 | Now → Apr 2027 (Prepare): commission the $0.45M third-party security and safety assessment now; negotiate the N term sheet with the M gates pre-agreed; tag customers so OEM/direct overlap can be measured.

Phase 1 | Apr 2027 → ~Q1 2028 (Option N: nonexclusive pilot): 12 months, $350 per shipped robot, no advance; Boreal keeps all direct and other-OEM rights; audit rights and monthly royalty reports from day one; existing licences untouched.

Phase 2 | Earliest ~Q2 2028 (Option M: limited exclusivity): new North American sales of the OEM's robot series only; up to 3 years, with an annual minimum royalty; automatic release if minimums are missed, the model is retired or certification lapses.
Phase 2 term: termination payment ≥ 1 year of displaced direct margin (~$1.5M).
All three gates must be passed before Phase 2. Each is verifiable by the board, not by OEM assertion.
Gate 1: Certification — ≥ 99.5% uptime in OEM production hardware in a fully loaded warehouse, including collision-heavy peaks; documented safe-stop; third-party assessment passed.

Gate 2: Verified demand — two consecutive audited quarters of ≥ 2,250 robots (~9,000/yr), at or above breakeven at 70% overlap (8,787 robots/yr). Accept the OEM's 5,000/yr gate only if other-OEM customers are carved out.
Gate 3: Contract protections — audit right, post-advance royalty floor, automatic release triggers, source code escrow, existing and other-OEM customers carved out, defined offset terms.
Negotiate by trading price, scope and timing for evidence, and walk away from any form of exclusivity that binds at signing.
Must-have (walk away without it): no exclusivity before Gates 1–3 are met.
Must-have: existing direct contracts excluded; exclusivity covers future new sales only.
Must-have: independent shipment audit right.
Must-have: source code escrow; no transfer of reusable IP.
Must-have: automatic release on model retirement or certification slip.
Tradeable (give to get) — royalty: concede from $350 toward $300 at conversion in return for a royalty floor.
Tradeable — volume gate: accept 5,000/yr instead of ~9,000 if the scope excludes other-OEM customers.
Tradeable — geography: narrower regions or named verticals first.
Tradeable — term: shorter initial exclusivity (e.g. 2 years) with renewal on performance.
Tradeable — an advance at conversion, structured as a capped and clearly defined guarantee.
Fallback if the OEM refuses (BATNA): continue direct sales: ~$1.8M new ARR in 2028, ~$1.48M gross margin.
Fallback: take the integration firm's nonexclusive 1,200-robot pilot ($0.22M support budget, no guarantee).
Fallback: complete certification anyway; return to the OEM with production evidence.
The fallback loses the OEM's upside (+$2.2–2.8M at plan) but avoids the low-case downside.
Leverage reality: Boreal's leverage is limited, but the OEM has itself put Options N and M on the table, and Boreal has not yet committed its IP.
Messaging: announce a 'strategic OEM partnership' now. Report any advance as a recoupable guarantee, never as revenue.
Four measurable signposts would change the recommendation, and the pilot is designed to produce all four.

Signpost — Verified OEM shipments. Today: unaudited forecast; no purchase orders. Move toward exclusivity if audited run-rate ≥ ~8,800 robots/yr: exclusivity pays even at 70% overlap. Move away from the OEM if run-rate < ~3,300/yr (N) or ~4,100/yr (X): royalties do not cover $0.9M engineering.

Signpost — Realised direct-channel overlap. Today: 0% (CEO) vs 30–70% (Sales); no customer IDs. Move toward exclusivity if measured ≤ 30%: breakeven falls to ~6,100 robots/yr. Move away if measured ≥ 70%: breakeven ~8,800/yr; insist on carving out other-OEM customers.

Signpost — Support cost per device. Today: $80 estimate. Move toward exclusivity if pilot confirms ≤ $80 and the $0.9M/yr engineering holds. Move away if above ~$107/robot: X loses value even at plan volume with 70% overlap (~$166 at 30%).

Signpost — Audit right. Today: absent from draft. Move toward exclusivity if shipment-level independent audit agreed and the first audit reconciles. No satisfactory audit right: no exclusivity at any reported volume.
Support-cost threshold: ($3.0M − $0.9M − overlap × $1.476M) ÷ 10,000 robots = $107 (70%) / $166 (30%) per robot.
The recommendation holds under the key assumptions; the main risk is that the OEM walks away, and the fallback limits that downside.
$0.9M/yr engineering for all of 2027–29 on every OEM route — conservative; equal across X/N/M.
30–70% overlap applied to the $1.8M direct ARR; 2028 cohort only in the base case — favours X (floor on the lost margin).
82% direct gross margin, before unquantified sales support — slightly overstates direct value.
The $0.45M assessment is needed for any OEM production route — neutral across OEM options.
No discounting; headroom counts deal cash only — per board; rest-of-business burn not in pack.
Risk: the OEM rejects N/M and signs with a competitor (limited leverage). Mitigation: M is the OEM's own proposal; trade price, scope and term; fallback is direct sales plus the integration pilot.
Risk: certification slips past September 2027. Mitigation: start the assessment now; release triggers; no exclusivity until passed.
Risk: support cost or engineering effort exceeds the estimate. Mitigation: measure in the pilot; reprice before conversion.
Risk: OEM volumes fall short of plan. Mitigation: Gate 2 uses audited volumes; royalty floor after conversion.
Risk: competitor claim proves causal after all. Mitigation: gated M still captures exclusivity benefits once proven.
Next steps: start certification now, since it is on the critical path for every OEM route, and bring the gated N→M term sheet to the April 2027 board.
Decision requested from the board (1): Reject Option X as drafted.
Decision requested from the board (2): Authorise management to negotiate Option N with the pre-agreed Option M gates and the must-have terms.
Decision requested from the board (3): Approve the $0.45M assessment now; this leaves $1.85M of headroom above the buffer.
Nov–Dec 2026: engage the third-party security and industrial-safety assessor ($0.45M). Proposed owner: CTO / Engineering. Output: signed scope; certification plan to September 2027.
Dec 2026–Mar 2027: add customer-level identifiers to the direct pipeline and OEM reports. Proposed owner: Sales + Finance. Output: baseline for measuring overlap.
Jan–Mar 2027: negotiate the N term sheet: audit, escrow, release, gates, carve-outs. Proposed owner: Partnerships + Legal. Output: term sheet for board approval.
Jan–Mar 2027: replace the CFO dashboard with a full incremental-margin view. Proposed owner: CFO. Output: royalty − $80/robot − $0.9M − displaced direct margin.
Apr 2027: board decision: approve N→M or a fallback. Owner: Board. Output: signed pilot, or direct + integration pilot.
Sep 2027: certification in OEM hardware (loaded warehouse, peak conditions). Proposed owner: Engineering. Output: Gate 1.
Q4 2027–Q1 2028: two audited quarters of OEM shipments; pilot support-cost readout. Proposed owner: Finance. Output: Gate 2 evidence.
~Q2 2028: gate review: convert to Option M, extend N or exit. Owner: Board. Output: exclusivity decision on evidence. (Owners are proposed.)

Appendix A, Plan ($M, 2027 / 2028 / 2029 / total): variable support ($80) −0.40 / −0.80 / −1.12 / −2.32; OEM engineering −0.90 / −0.90 / −0.90 / −2.70; OEM contribution 0.20 / 1.30 / 2.18 / 3.68; security/safety assessment −0.45; value before channel effects 3.23.

Appendix A, 65% stress ($M, 2027 / 2028 / 2029 / total): variable support −0.26 / −0.52 / −0.73 / −1.51; OEM engineering −0.90 / −0.90 / −0.90 / −2.70; OEM contribution −0.19 / 0.53 / 1.10 / 1.45; assessment −0.45; value before channel effects 1.00.
Lost direct GM, 30% / 70% (2028 cohort only): −0.44 / −1.03 in both cases; exclusivity value 30% / 70%: plan 2.79 / 2.20; stress 0.55 / −0.04 ($M).
Direct gross margin at risk = $1.8M new 2028 ARR × 82% = $1.476M; × 30% = $0.44M; × 70% = $1.03M. Totals may differ by ±0.01 due to rounding.
Formulas: Royalty cash (X) = royalties earned − advance credit still unrecouped (first $2.0M of royalties); OEM contribution = robots × (royalty − $80) − $0.9M engineering per year.
Data gap — channel overlap: no customer-level data. We used Sales' 30–70% range, bounded by 0% and 100%.
Data gap — direct churn and later cohorts: not in the pack. The base case counts the 2028 cohort only; a 2029 renewal sensitivity is on slide 6.
Data gap — OEM enforcement terms and termination payment: not in the pack. Treated qualitatively.
Data gap — pricing under N/M: the OEM will not guarantee it. Shown as indicative.
